1.pericope_label: So they brought the ark of God, and set it in the midst of the tent that David had pitched for it: and they offered burnt sacrifices and peace offerings before God. And when David had made an end of offering the burnt offerings and the peace offerings, he blessed the people in the name of the Lord. And he dealt to every one of Israel, both man and woman, to every one a loaf of bread, and a good piece of flesh, and a flagon of wine. And he appointed certain of the Levites to minister before the ark of the Lord, and to record, and to thank and praise the Lord God of Israel: Asaph the chief, and next to him Zechariah, Jeiel, and Shemiramoth, and Jehiel, and Mattithiah, and Eliab, and Benaiah, and Obed–edom: and Jeiel with psalteries and with harps; but Asaph made a sound with cymbals; Benaiah also and Jahaziel the priests with trumpets continually before the ark of the covenant of God.

schools.summary: Ellicott protests the chapter division, collects the small departures from the parallel in Samuel and finds an editorial pattern in them, and parses each item of the distribution, denying that the third gift is wine at all; Delitzsch joins him in treating "to record" as a technical term keyed to the psalm superscriptions.
Gill corrects the roster, noting that Asaph is chief only of those now appointed, Heman being chief of the three principal singers.

Clarke sets the Targum against Ellicott on the gifts, making them the sixth part of an ox and the sixth part of a hin of wine; Wesley draws the practical inference that all our rejoicings should express themselves in thanksgivings.
Henry measures the day against what the ark had come from and what it still lacked, and judges David's tent a better thing than Solomon's temple, since the church's poorest times were its purest.

debates: What David distributed to the people: Ellicott makes the third gift a raisin-cake and doubts the second, while the Targum Clarke reports makes them a sixth of an ox and a sixth of a hin of wine.
Whether the chronicler's wording at the sacrifices is a deliberate adjustment to show that priests and Levites ministered, as Ellicott argues.
outliers: Ellicott suggests the divine title Sabaoth is dropped from the blessing because it had grown obsolete in the chronicler's day.
themes: So they brought the ark of God, and set it in the midst of the tent that David had pitched for it: and they offered burnt sacrifices and peace offerings before God.
And when David had made an end of offering the burnt offerings and the peace offerings, he blessed the people in the name of the Lord.
And he dealt to every one of Israel, both man and woman, to every one a loaf of bread, and a good piece of flesh, and a flagon of wine.
And he appointed certain of the Levites to minister before the ark of the Lord, and to record, and to thank and praise the Lord God of Israel:

Asaph the chief, and next to him Zechariah, Jeiel, and Shemiramoth, and Jehiel, and Mattithiah, and Eliab, and Benaiah, and Obed–edom: and Jeiel with psalteries and with harps; but Asaph made a sound with cymbals;
Benaiah also and Jahaziel the priests with trumpets continually before the ark of the covenant of God.

7.pericope_label: Then on that day David delivered first this psalm to thank the Lord into the hand of Asaph and his brethren. Give thanks unto the Lord, call upon his name, make known his deeds among the people. Sing unto him, sing psalms unto him, talk ye of all his wondrous works. Glory ye in his holy name: let the heart of them rejoice that seek the Lord. Seek the Lord and his strength, seek his face continually. Remember his marvellous works that he hath done, his wonders, and the judgments of his mouth; O ye seed of Israel his servant, ye children of Jacob, his chosen ones. He is the Lord our God; his judgments are in all the earth. Be ye mindful always of his covenant; the word which he commanded to a thousand generations; Even of the covenant which he made with Abraham, and of his oath unto Isaac; And hath confirmed the same to Jacob for a law, and to Israel for an everlasting covenant, Saying, Unto thee will I give the land of Canaan, the lot of your inheritance; When ye were but few, even a few, and strangers in it. And when they went from nation to nation, and from one kingdom to another people; He suffered no man to do them wrong: yea, he reproved kings for their sakes, Saying, Touch not mine anointed, and do my prophets no harm.

schools.summary: Ellicott builds four arguments that the ode is a later insertion rather than original to the book, and supports them with a running demonstration that this text is secondary to the Psalter's at a dozen points; Delitzsch flatly contradicts the first of those arguments, holding the hymn a connected and uniform whole and setting out its movement to prove it.

Clarke takes the verse plainly, that David made the psalm on this occasion and gave it to Asaph, and allows the title "mine anointed" to the whole people; Wesley reads "first" as first of a series, implying many psalms delivered afterwards.
Henry sets out the same cento openly, treats the psalm as composed earlier by David and only now handed to Asaph, and infers that we are warranted to make up hymns out of parts of several psalms.

debates: Whether the ode is Davidic and original to Chronicles or a later compiler's substitute drawn from the Psalter.
Whether the hymn is a connected and uniform whole, as Delitzsch holds, or so loosely patched that the seams are visible, as Ellicott argues.
What "first" means in verse 7: the first delivery of this psalm, the first of many psalms, or the first charging of Asaph with the duty of thanksgiving.
outliers: Ellicott marks the seam exactly, where the older psalm would have gone on to Egypt and the Exodus and instead stops dead so that a fresh start can be made.
themes: Then on that day David delivered first this psalm to thank the Lord into the hand of Asaph and his brethren.
Give thanks unto the Lord, call upon his name, make known his deeds among the people.
Sing unto him, sing psalms unto him, talk ye of all his wondrous works.
Glory ye in his holy name: let the heart of them rejoice that seek the Lord.
Seek the Lord and his strength, seek his face continually.
Remember his marvellous works that he hath done, his wonders, and the judgments of his mouth;
O ye seed of Israel his servant, ye children of Jacob, his chosen ones.
He is the Lord our God; his judgments are in all the earth.
Be ye mindful always of his covenant; the word which he commanded to a thousand generations;
Even of the covenant which he made with Abraham, and of his oath unto Isaac;
And hath confirmed the same to Jacob for a law, and to Israel for an everlasting covenant,
Saying, Unto thee will I give the land of Canaan, the lot of your inheritance;
When ye were but few, even a few, and strangers in it.
And when they went from nation to nation, and from one kingdom to another people;
He suffered no man to do them wrong: yea, he reproved kings for their sakes,
Saying, Touch not mine anointed, and do my prophets no harm.

31.pericope_label: Let the heavens be glad, and let the earth rejoice: and let men say among the nations, The Lord reigneth.

schools.summary: Clarke is the only witness on this verse, and reports that the Targum turns the glad heavens into the supreme angels, using the Greek word for angels written out in Hebrew letters.

debates: Whether the summons is to the heavens themselves or, as the Targum has it, to the angelic host.
outliers: The Targumist reaches past his own language for a Greek loanword, which dates his idiom by the borrowing.
themes: Let the heavens be glad, and let the earth rejoice: and let men say among the nations, The Lord reigneth.

34.pericope_label: O give thanks unto the Lord; for he is good; for his mercy endureth for ever. And say ye, Save us, O God of our salvation, and gather us together, and deliver us from the heathen, that we may give thanks to thy holy name, and glory in thy praise.

schools.summary: Ellicott identifies the opening call as the liturgic formula several later psalms begin with, and observes that the ode thus ends with the thought it started from.
Gill holds that David wrote the petition by a spirit of prophecy, foreseeing the dispersion, but records the alternative that these verses were added by Ezra.

Clarke takes the verse devotionally, making a rule of praying to God under the attribute whose influence is needed; Wesley agrees with Gill that the psalm was written for future ages in which Israel would be scattered.
Henry reads it as the reminder that praise must not crowd out prayer for afflicted brethren, since we are members one of another.

debates: Whether the closing petition is David's by prophetic foresight or a later addition made after the captivity.
outliers: Clarke sets out a pattern for the practice: being weak we appeal to the Almighty, being ignorant to the Father of lights, being lost to the merciful God.
themes: O give thanks unto the Lord; for he is good; for his mercy endureth for ever.
And say ye, Save us, O God of our salvation, and gather us together, and deliver us from the heathen, that we may give thanks to thy holy name, and glory in thy praise.

37.pericope_label: So he left there before the ark of the covenant of the Lord Asaph and his brethren, to minister before the ark continually, as every day’s work required: And Obed–edom with their brethren, threescore and eight; Obed–edom also the son of Jeduthun and Hosah to be porters: And Zadok the priest, and his brethren the priests, before the tabernacle of the Lord in the high place that was at Gibeon, To offer burnt offerings unto the Lord upon the altar of the burnt offering continually morning and evening, and to do according to all that is written in the law of the Lord, which he commanded Israel; And with them Heman and Jeduthun, and the rest that were chosen, who were expressed by name, to give thanks to the Lord, because his mercy endureth for ever; And with them Heman and Jeduthun with trumpets and cymbals for those that should make a sound, and with musical instruments of God. And the sons of Jeduthun were porters. And all the people departed every man to his house: and David returned to bless his house.

schools.summary: Delitzsch explains why no priest is named at the tent of the ark, finds a dropped name behind the plural "their brethren", and joins Ellicott in reading the omission of the Michal episode as the exclusion of a domestic matter from a history of sacred institutions.

Clarke turns the phrase "instruments of God" into a sustained argument that instrumental music in Christian worship is antichristian; Wesley takes the same phrase the opposite way, as instruments appropriated to God's worship and marking the difference between common mirth and holy joy.

Henry admits he cannot conceive why David left the ark and the altar apart, guesses that the Mosaic curtains were too worn to move, and reads the Jerusalem service as spiritual worship taking place of ceremonial.

debates: Why the ark and the altar were left in separate places throughout David's reign, which Henry confesses he cannot explain.
Whether "instruments of God" licenses instrumental worship or, as Clarke argues from the versions and especially the Syriac, tells against it.
How the Obed-edom of verse 38 relates to the Obed-edom called son of Jeduthun, given that the name also appears among singers and among doorkeepers.
outliers: Clarke asks whether mere sounds, uttering no word or sentiment, can be counted praise at all, and calls the argument from Jewish use futile in the extreme when applied to Christianity.
themes: So he left there before the ark of the covenant of the Lord Asaph and his brethren, to minister before the ark continually, as every day’s work required:
And Obed–edom with their brethren, threescore and eight; Obed–edom also the son of Jeduthun and Hosah to be porters:
And Zadok the priest, and his brethren the priests, before the tabernacle of the Lord in the high place that was at Gibeon,

To offer burnt offerings unto the Lord upon the altar of the burnt offering continually morning and evening, and to do according to all that is written in the law of the Lord, which he commanded Israel;
And with them Heman and Jeduthun, and the rest that were chosen, who were expressed by name, to give thanks to the Lord, because his mercy endureth for ever;
And with them Heman and Jeduthun with trumpets and cymbals for those that should make a sound, and with musical instruments of God. And the sons of Jeduthun were porters.
